title: UNIT 3: IMPORTANT INORGANIC COMPOUNDS
notes: ✓ Important inorganic compounds are mainly classified as oxides, acids, bases and salts.

title: 3.1 Introduction to Inorganic Compounds
notes: ✓ Inorganic compounds mainly originate from mineral constituents of the Earth's crust and include oxides, acids, bases and salts.

title: 3.2 Oxides
notes:
✓ OXIDES → Binary compounds containing oxygen combined with another element such as a metal, non-metal or metalloid.

◆ MAIN TYPES
✓ Acidic oxides.
✓ Basic oxides.
✓ Amphoteric oxides.
✓ Neutral oxides.
✓ Peroxides.

◆ EXAMPLES
MgO, Al₂O₃, CO₂, SO₂ and CO.

title: 3.2.1 Acidic Oxides
notes:
✓ ACIDIC OXIDES → Generally oxides of non-metals. They are also called acid anhydrides because they can form acids with water.

◆ EXAMPLES
CO₂, SO₂, NO₂, N₂O₅ and P₄O₁₀.

◆ IMPORTANT REACTIONS
CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃
SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃

→ Acidic oxides also react with bases or basic oxides to form salts.

title: 3.2.2 Basic Oxides
notes:
✓ BASIC OXIDES → Generally metallic oxides. Some dissolve in water to form alkaline solutions, while insoluble basic oxides react with acids to form salt and water.

◆ EXAMPLES
Li₂O, Na₂O, K₂O, MgO, CaO, BaO and CuO.

◆ IMPORTANT REACTIONS
CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂
CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O
Na₂O + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃

→ Basic oxides react with acidic oxides and acids to form salts.

title: 3.2.3 Amphoteric Oxides
notes:
✓ AMPHOTERIC OXIDES → Show both acidic and basic properties. They react with strong acids as well as strong bases to form salts and water or related products.

◆ EXAMPLES
Al₂O₃, ZnO, PbO, PbO₂, SnO and SnO₂.

✓ Amphoteric hydroxide example: Al(OH)₃.

◆ REMEMBER
Amphoteric → Reacts with both acids and bases.

title: 3.2.4 Neutral Oxides
notes:
✓ NEUTRAL OXIDES → Do not show acidic or basic properties and generally do not react with acids or bases to form salt and water.

◆ EXAMPLES
H₂O
CO
N₂O
NO

→ Neutral oxides are not salt-forming oxides.

title: 3.2.5 Peroxides
notes:
✓ PEROXIDES → Contain an O–O bond, and oxygen has an oxidation number of −1.

◆ EXAMPLES
H₂O₂
Na₂O₂
CaO₂
BaO₂

→ Peroxides are generally powerful oxidizing agents and can react by releasing oxygen.

title: 3.3 Acids
notes:
✓ According to the Arrhenius definition, an acid releases H⁺ or H₃O⁺ ions in aqueous solution.

◆ GENERAL IONIZATION
HA(aq) → H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq)

◆ EXAMPLES
HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, H₃PO₄, HBr, HI and HF.

title: 3.3.1 Classification of Acids
notes:
✓ Acids can be classified according to the number of ionizable hydrogen atoms and the number of elements present.

◆ BY IONIZABLE H⁺
✓ Monoprotic acid → One ionizable H⁺, e.g. HCl.
✓ Polyprotic acid → More than one ionizable H⁺.
✓ Diprotic acid → Two ionizable H⁺, e.g. H₂SO₄.

◆ BY NUMBER OF ELEMENTS
✓ Binary acids → Contain two elements.
✓ Ternary acids → Contain three elements.

title: 3.3.2 Strong and Weak Acids
notes:
✓ STRONG ACIDS → Completely ionize in aqueous solution and produce a large concentration of H⁺ ions.
Examples: HCl, HNO₃ and H₂SO₄.

✓ WEAK ACIDS → Ionize only partially and exist mainly in non-ionized form.
Example: CH₃COOH.

→ Strong/weak describes the degree of ionization, not the concentration.

title: 3.3.3 Concentrated and Dilute Acids
notes:
✓ CONCENTRATED ACID → Contains a relatively large amount of acid per unit volume of solution.

✓ DILUTE ACID → Contains a smaller amount of acid per unit volume of solution.

◆ IMPORTANT DISTINCTION
✓ Strong → Degree of ionization.
✓ Concentrated → Amount of acid in a given volume.
✓ Weak → Partial ionization.
✓ Dilute → Lower concentration.

title: 3.3.4 Indicators and pH
notes:
✓ Indicators help identify whether a solution is acidic or basic.

◆ COMMON INDICATORS
✓ Litmus → Acid: red; base: blue.
✓ Phenolphthalein → Acid: colourless; base: pink.
✓ Methyl orange → Acid: red; base: yellow.
✓ Universal indicator → Shows different colours over the pH scale.

✓ pH = −log[H⁺]

◆ AT 25°C
Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴
pH + pOH = 14.

title: 3.3.5 Chemical Properties and Preparation of Acids
notes:
✓ Acids react with active metals to produce salts and hydrogen gas:
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂

✓ Acids also react with bases and metallic oxides to form salts and water, and with carbonates to form salt, water and CO₂.

◆ PREPARATION OF ACIDS
✓ Acidic oxide + water → Acid.
✓ Non-metal + hydrogen → Binary acid.
✓ Formation of volatile acids from non-volatile acids.

title: 3.4 Bases
notes:
✓ According to Arrhenius, a base produces OH⁻ ions when dissolved in water. Soluble bases are called alkalis.

◆ EXAMPLES
NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻
KOH → K⁺ + OH⁻

✓ Ammonia acts as a base by reacting with water:
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻.

title: 3.4.1 Strong and Weak Bases
notes:
✓ STRONG BASES → Ionize almost completely in aqueous solution and produce large amounts of OH⁻ ions.

✓ WEAK BASES → Ionize only partially.

◆ EXAMPLES OF STRONG BASES
NaOH and KOH.

→ Concentrated and dilute describe the amount of base in a given volume, while strong and weak describe the degree of ionization.

✓ Strong bases such as NaOH and KOH are corrosive and poisonous.

title: 3.4.2 Properties and Preparation of Bases
notes:
✓ Bases generally have a bitter taste and a slippery or soapy feel.
✓ They react with acids in neutralization reactions.

◆ PREPARATION OF BASES
✓ Active metal + water → Metal hydroxide + H₂.
✓ Basic oxide + water → Metal hydroxide.
✓ Double displacement reactions.

◆ EXAMPLES
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH

◆ USES
✓ NaOH → Soaps, detergents, degreasers and cleaners.
✓ Ca(OH)₂ → Cement, lime water and neutralizing acidic soil.

title: 3.4.3 pOH
notes:
✓ pOH measures hydroxide-ion concentration.

pOH = −log[OH⁻]

◆ AT 25°C
pH + pOH = 14

◆ THEREFORE
pH = 14 − pOH
pOH = 14 − pH

◆ EXAMPLE
If [OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M:
pOH = 4
pH = 10.

title: 3.5 Salts
notes:
✓ SALTS → Ionic compounds generally formed by neutralization of an acid with a base. They contain a cation derived from a base and an anion derived from an acid.

◆ GENERAL REACTION
Acid + Base → Salt + Water

◆ EXAMPLE
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

→ Salts are also formed when ionizable hydrogen atoms of acids are partly or completely replaced by metal or ammonium ions.

title: 3.5.1 Classification of Salts
notes:
◆ THREE MAIN GROUPS

✓ NORMAL SALTS → All ionizable H⁺ ions are completely replaced by metal or NH₄⁺ ions.
Examples: NaCl, KCl.

✓ ACIDIC SALTS → Only some ionizable H⁺ ions are replaced.
Examples: KHSO₄, NaH₂PO₄.

✓ BASIC SALTS → Not all OH⁻ ions of a polyhydroxy base are replaced by acid anions.
Examples: Al(OH)₂Cl, Zn(OH)NO₃.

title: 3.5.2 Preparation of Salts
notes:
✓ Soluble salts are generally prepared by crystallization, while insoluble salts are prepared by precipitation.

◆ MAIN METHODS
✓ Active metal + acid → Salt + H₂.
✓ Acid + base → Salt + H₂O.
✓ Metallic oxide + acid → Salt + H₂O.
✓ Carbonate/bicarbonate + acid → Salt + H₂O + CO₂.
✓ Double decomposition of soluble salts → Insoluble precipitate.

◆ EXAMPLE
Na₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

title: 3.5.3 Properties of Salts
notes:
✓ Salts may be soluble, insoluble or slightly soluble in water.
✓ Aqueous solutions of soluble salts conduct electricity because they contain mobile ions.

◆ BASED ON INTERACTION WITH ATMOSPHERIC MOISTURE
✓ Hygroscopic → Absorbs water but remains solid.
✓ Deliquescent → Absorbs water and forms a solution.
✓ Efflorescent → Loses water of crystallization to the atmosphere.

◆ EXAMPLES
CaCl₂ → Deliquescent.
Anhydrous CuSO₄ → Hygroscopic.
Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Efflorescent.

title: 3.5.4 Thermal Decomposition of Salts
notes:
✓ Some salts decompose when heated.

✓ MOST METAL CARBONATES:
Metal carbonate → Metal oxide + CO₂

✓ MOST GROUP IIA AND TRANSITION-METAL NITRATES:
Nitrate → Metal oxide + NO₂ + O₂

◆ SODIUM AND POTASSIUM NITRATES
2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂
2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂

→ Lithium salts show different thermal decomposition behavior.

title: 3.5.5 Chemical Tests of Ions in Salts
notes:
✓ Several tests are used to identify ions in salts.

✓ Flame tests → Identify some metal ions such as Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺ and Ba²⁺ by characteristic flame colours.
✓ Halide ions → Can be tested using silver nitrate.
✓ Sulphate ions → Can be tested using acidified barium reagent.
✓ Nitrate ions → Can be tested by the appropriate reduction test.
✓ Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions → Have characteristic reactions with suitable reagents.

title: 3.5.6 Important Salts and Uses
notes:
◆ IMPORTANT SALTS AND APPLICATIONS

✓ NaCl → Source for sodium, chlorine and NaOH; ORS component; manufacture of NaHCO₃ and Na₂CO₃.

✓ NH₄NO₃ → Nitrogen fertilizer.

✓ CuSO₄ → Bordeaux mixture, fungicides, electroplating and dyeing.

✓ FeCl₃ → Wastewater treatment and printed-circuit etching.

✓ KNO₃ → Fertilizer and other industrial uses.

✓ CaSO₄·2H₂O (gypsum) → Plastering and supporting fractured bones.

✓ BaSO₄ → Barium meal for gastrointestinal X-rays and white pigment.

✓ FeSO₄ → Iron tablets for anemia.

title: Plant Nutrients, Fertilizers and Pesticides
notes:
✓ Plant nutrients are classified as macronutrients and micronutrients.

✓ MACRONUTRIENTS → N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S, C, H and O.
✓ MICRONUTRIENTS → Fe, Co, Zn, Mn, Mo, Cu, B and Cl.

◆ PRIMARY MINERAL NUTRIENTS
✓ N → Amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll.
✓ P → Root development, maturity, seeds/fruits and ATP.
✓ K → Enzyme activity, photosynthesis, protein synthesis and cell turgidity.

title: Fertilizers and NPK
notes:
✓ FERTILIZERS → Materials added to soil to increase crop growth, yield or nutritional value.

✓ Organic fertilizers come from plants and animals.
✓ Synthetic fertilizers commonly supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

✓ NPK → Nitrogen + Phosphorus + Potassium.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ (NH₄)₂SO₄
✓ KNO₃
✓ NH₄NO₃
✓ DAP, (NH₄)₂HPO₄

✓ A fertilizer grade such as 10:10:10 indicates 10% N, 10% P and 10% K by dry weight.

title: Pesticides and Herbicides
notes:
✓ PESTICIDES → Chemicals used to kill pests that affect plant growth and development.

✓ HERBICIDES → Weed killers used to control undesirable plants.

◆ EXAMPLES OF HERBICIDAL SALTS
NaCl, CuSO₄, NaAsO₂, ammonium sulphamate and NaClO₃.

title: UNIT 3 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
◆ OXIDES
✓ Acidic → Generally non-metal oxides.
✓ Basic → Generally metal oxides.
✓ Amphoteric → Reacts with both acids and bases.
✓ Neutral → Neither acidic nor basic.
✓ Peroxide → Contains O–O bond; O = −1.

◆ ACIDS
✓ pH = −log[H⁺]
✓ Strong acid → Almost complete ionization.
✓ Weak acid → Partial ionization.

◆ BASES
✓ pOH = −log[OH⁻]
✓ pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C.
✓ Strong base → Almost complete ionization.

◆ SALTS
✓ Acid + Base → Salt + Water.
✓ Normal salt → Complete replacement of ionizable H⁺.
✓ Acidic salt → Partial replacement of ionizable H⁺.
✓ Basic salt → Contains ionizable OH⁻.

◆ PLANT NUTRIENTS
✓ N → Growth and chlorophyll.
✓ P → Roots, maturity and seeds/fruits.
✓ K → Enzymes, photosynthesis and cell turgidity.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Do not confuse strong/weak with concentrated/dilute.
→ Strong and weak describe ionization, while concentrated and dilute describe the amount of solute in a given volume.
